explain.say: Press a ballpoint pen, sit in a car, close a valve in an engine: a helical spring pushes back each time. Look at the spring: a steel wire 5 millimetres thick, wound into 10 active coils of 40 millimetre mean diameter, with a 300 newton load on top.

draw.text: Helical springs: stiffness, coil stress and the Wahl factor

parts.label: Spring, 10 coils
parts.ask: How does a coil spring carry load?

draw.text: d = 5 mm wire, D = 40 mm coil, n = 10 active coils, steel G = 79 GPa

explain.say: When you squash a coil spring, the wire actually twists. So its stiffness comes from the shear modulus G. The spring rate k is G d to the fourth over 8 D cubed n. Plug in: 79 gigapascals, 5 millimetre wire, 40 millimetre coils, 10 coils, gives 9.64 newtons per millimetre. Which change makes the biggest difference?

explain.say: Wire diameter, because it is to the fourth power: a 6 millimetre wire would make the spring twice as stiff. Now the graph. Force is k times deflection, a straight line. Our 300 newtons squashes the spring 31.1 millimetres. See the steeper line? Fewer coils, 8 instead of 10, make it stiffer: 12.05.

explain.say: Now the stress in the wire. The basic twist stress is 8 F D over pi d cubed. But the wire is curved, so the inside of each coil is stressed more. The spring index C, D over d, is 8 here, and the Wahl factor corrects for curvature: 1.18. So the stress is about 289 megapascals. Is that safe for spring steel?

explain.say: Yes, spring steel wire is very strong, so this has a good margin. Lovely work! Exam tip: keep the spring index between about 4 and 12. Too low and the wire is hard to coil; too high and the spring buckles and tangles. Challenge: two identical springs in series: what is the combined k?

faq.q: How does a coil spring carry load?
faq.a: When you compress a helical spring, each part of the wire twists like a little torsion bar. That is why the shear modulus G sets its stiffness.

faq.q: How do I calculate the stiffness of a coil spring?
faq.a: Spring rate k equals G d to the fourth over 8 D cubed n, where d is wire diameter, D the mean coil diameter and n the number of active coils.
asks: what does the number of coils do

faq.a: C equals D over d, the mean coil diameter over the wire diameter. Good springs usually have C between about 4 and 12.

faq.q: What is the Wahl correction factor?
faq.a: A factor that raises the calculated shear stress to allow for wire curvature and direct shear: K w equals 4C minus 1 over 4C minus 4, plus 0.615 over C.

faq.q: How do springs combine in series and parallel?
faq.a: In parallel the stiffnesses add. In series the reciprocals add, so two identical springs in series have half the stiffness of one.

facts: Spring stiffness rises with the fourth power of wire diameter.
Fewer active coils make a spring stiffer: k is inversely proportional to n.
